prompt: What does a CIS Benchmark recommendation carry besides the setting itself?
hint: Think of what settles an argument with a colleague.

choices.text: A script that applies every recommendation of the guide in one go
choices.why: The guide describes remediation per item; applying everything blind is what it warns against.

choices.text: Its rationale, the audit that proves it, and its impact on the machine
choices.why: Right. The rationale argues it, the audit proves it, the impact says what it may cost.

choices.text: The name of the volunteer who wrote it and the date it was agreed
choices.why: Benchmarks are agreed by consensus; no recommendation is signed.

choices.text: A severity score from 0 to 10
choices.why: That is CVSS, for vulnerabilities, in lesson 16.

prompt: What separates a Level 2 recommendation from a Level 1 one?

choices.text: Level 2 applies to servers and Level 1 to workstations
choices.why: Both levels exist for servers and for workstations, as the four profiles showed.

choices.text: Level 2 settings are checked by machine and Level 1 by a person
choices.why: Both have an audit command.

choices.text: Level 2 costs some machines a function
choices.why: Right. Level 1 is meant to be safe everywhere; Level 2 is defence in depth with a price.

choices.text: Level 2 is the newer edition, which replaces Level 1
choices.why: They are two profiles of the same edition, not two editions.

prompt: Why does CIS publish one Benchmark for Ubuntu 22.04 and another for 24.04?

choices.text: Paths, packages and defaults change between releases
choices.why: Right. An audit written for one release can be wrong on the next.

choices.text: Each release is sold under a separate licence that the guide has to cite
choices.why: Ubuntu is free software; licences have nothing to do with it.

choices.text: So that each one can be paid for separately by members
choices.why: The PDFs are free after registering.

choices.text: Because 24.04 needs no hardening of the kind 22.04 did
choices.why: Every release needs one; the guide changes because the system did.

prompt: Two servers both score 69 on Lynis's hardening index. What can you conclude?
hint: What is the index useful against?

choices.text: That they are equally safe and need the same changes
choices.why: The same score can come from completely different failures.

choices.text: That both pass CIS Level 1, which starts at 65
choices.why: Lynis's index is its own arithmetic, not a CIS threshold.

choices.text: Very little: the index compares a machine with itself
choices.why: Right. Before and after a change on one machine is what it measures.

choices.text: That each has 31 failed tests
choices.why: The index is weighted; it is not a count of failures.

prompt: Lynis warns that two name servers do not respond on web. What is the right reading?

choices.text: The portal is under attack and its resolvers were taken down
choices.why: Nothing points to an attack: the lab has no route to the internet.

choices.text: A true finding about the lab, not about the portal
choices.why: Right. Reading a warning is deciding which kind it is.

choices.text: A false positive that should be reported to the Lynis authors
choices.why: It is true: those servers do not answer from inside the lab.

choices.text: A reason to install a second resolver on web itself
choices.why: A resolver with nothing to ask would not answer either.

prompt: Lynis raised eight warnings on the portal and none about its FTP server or its SNMP community `public`. Why?
hint: What does an auditor not know about your machine?

choices.text: Its quick mode skips network services
choices.why: --quick only skips the pauses between sections.

choices.text: Those services were already disabled when it ran
choices.why: They were running: lesson 1 found them on the same image.

choices.text: It cannot know the portal's job needs two ports
choices.why: Right. Only you know the job, which is why the baseline is yours.

choices.text: FTP and SNMP are outside the scope of any configuration guide
choices.why: CIS covers removing unneeded services, FTP and SNMP included.

prompt: OpenSCAP returns `notapplicable` for all 291 rules of the 22.04 CIS profile on web. What did it test?

choices.text: Nothing on the machine's configuration, because no rule ran at all
choices.why: Right. The platform check failed first, so no test ran.

choices.text: Every rule, and all of them happened not to apply to a portal
choices.why: Not applicable came from the release, not from the portal's job.

choices.text: Only the rules about packages, because the others need root
choices.why: It ran with sudo; the platform, not privilege, stopped it.

choices.text: The 24.04 rules, which the package stores under the 22.04 name
choices.why: The package has no 24.04 content at all.

prompt: A colleague proposes editing the platform line of the 22.04 data stream so OpenSCAP accepts web. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Nothing; the rules are close enough between releases
choices.why: Close enough is exactly what makes results wrong without saying so.

choices.text: The results would look real and mean nothing
choices.why: Right. Rules would test moved files and pass on renamed packages.

choices.text: It breaks the package's signature, so apt refuses every update afterwards
choices.why: apt does not verify installed files on update; the harm is the meaningless results.

choices.text: OpenSCAP keeps a hash of each file and will refuse to load it
choices.why: It would load it and run every rule, which is the problem.

prompt: Match each SCAP standard with what it describes.

pairs.right: a checklist of rules grouped into profiles
how to test one rule on a machine
the name of a platform a rule applies to

right_distractors: a score for the severity of a flaw

prompt: Why does `no_telnet` ask what listens on port 23 instead of reading /etc/inetd.conf?

choices.text: Because /etc/inetd.conf can only be read by root
choices.why: The script runs as root anyway.

choices.text: A telnet server started any other way fails it too
choices.why: Right. Ask about the effect, not the file meant to produce it.

choices.text: Because ss is faster than reading a configuration file from disk
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; both take milliseconds.

choices.text: Because inetd.conf is removed when inetd is purged
choices.why: Then reading it would pass, which is the point: the file is not the effect.

prompt: check.sh ends with `exit $fail`. What does that make possible?

choices.text: Running the check without root
choices.why: It still needs root to read sshd -T and passwd -S.

choices.text: Stopping at the first failed control so the rest are not tested
choices.why: Every control runs; the count comes at the end.

choices.text: Printing each failure in a colour the terminal shows in red
choices.why: It prints no colours; the exit status is for programs.

choices.text: Another program reads the verdict from it
choices.why: Right. A check a program can read is a check that can run every night.

prompt: Why does each control carry an id such as JAT-04 instead of being numbered by its line?

choices.text: So reports stay comparable after a control is added
choices.why: Right. Positions shift; a written id does not.

choices.text: Because Lynis requires ids in that format to read the script
choices.why: Lynis never reads check.sh.

choices.text: Because bash functions cannot be numbered
choices.why: The ids are labels in the output, not function names.

choices.text: To hide from an attacker which controls the firm has decided on
choices.why: Each id is printed beside a plain sentence saying what it means.

prompt: What does `ansible -m ping` prove before the playbook runs?

choices.text: That the machine answers ICMP echo requests
choices.why: It is not a network ping at all.

choices.text: The network path, the SSH key and Python on the far side
choices.why: Right. It logs in over SSH and runs a small Python program.

choices.text: That every task in the playbook will succeed when it runs
choices.why: It proves the connection, not the tasks.

choices.text: That the inventory file has no syntax errors anywhere in it
choices.why: It would fail on a bad inventory, but that is not what it is for.

prompt: The second run of harden.yml reports changed=0. Why does that matter before you schedule it?

choices.text: It proves the portal is now fully hardened against every guide
choices.why: It proves the playbook is stable, not that the baseline is complete.

choices.text: It means Ansible cached the results and skipped the work
choices.why: Every task ran and checked the state; nothing needed changing.

choices.text: A run that is safe to repeat touches nothing that is already right
choices.why: Right. That is idempotence, and only an idempotent playbook should run unattended.

choices.text: It shows the handlers ran a second time without errors
choices.why: No handler ran: nothing notified them.

prompt: What does `validate: /usr/sbin/sshd -t -f %s` do in the SSH task?

choices.text: Tests the new file before it replaces anything
choices.why: Right. A typo in the playbook never reaches the server.

choices.text: Restarts sshd and rolls back if the restart fails
choices.why: Reloading is the handler's job, and nothing is rolled back.

choices.text: Prints the effective configuration after the change
choices.why: That is sshd -T; -t only checks.

choices.text: Checks that the file was signed by the administrator who wrote the playbook
choices.why: Nothing is signed; it is a syntax check.

prompt: After 05-quickfix.conf is added, why does the playbook still report changed=0?
hint: What was it asked to make true?

choices.text: Because Ansible does not run tasks it has already run once
choices.why: It runs every task every time and checks each state.

choices.text: Because sshd was not reloaded after the new file appeared
choices.why: Reloading has nothing to do with it: the playbook never looks at that file.

choices.text: Its own file is still right, and it manages no other
choices.why: Right. The check, which asks sshd -T, is what notices.

choices.text: Because the quick fix is a valid sshd setting
choices.why: Valid or not, the playbook would never have read it.

prompt: After `skip-test=FILE-6310`, the hardening index went from 69 to 66. What does that say about the machine?

choices.text: It is less secure, because a test is no longer run
choices.why: Nothing on the machine changed; only what was counted did.

choices.text: Nothing about the machine: only what Lynis counted changed
choices.why: Right. The index is arithmetic, up or down.

choices.text: That skipping tests is forbidden by the CIS licence
choices.why: Lynis is not CIS, and skipping a test is a documented feature.

choices.text: That /home must be moved to its own partition after all
choices.why: The decision stands; a score does not overturn it.

prompt: Which of these belong in a written exception? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: What covers the risk instead
choices.why: The compensating control.

choices.text: Who decided, and until when
choices.why: Without an expiry an exception becomes permanent by default.

choices.text: The hardening index before and after the skip
choices.why: The index says nothing about the decision.

choices.text: Why the control does not fit this machine
choices.why: The reason is what an auditor asks.
